'''Gorodovaya Syndikalizm''' is a radical variant of [[Syndicalism]] associated with the industrial city or state of [[Vorkutangrad]].

The old source uses the shorter form Vorkuta, while the 2003 and 2022 map references use Vorkutangrad. This draft treats Vorkuta as a source short form, older city name, or internal name for Vorkutangrad pending final canon review.

== Origins ==

The ideology was first formulated by [[Viktor Zheleznyakov]], a former industrial planner who argued in ''The City Belongs to All'' in 1923 that ordinary workplace syndicalism was not enough for modern industrial cities.

Gorodovaya Syndikalizm gained traction during the [[Vorkutan Labor Crisis]] of 1924-1926. Under [[Marina Volkhova]], worker assemblies took control of industrial districts and developed the kollektiv system.

== Doctrine ==

The ideology treats city, factory, housing, transport, and public services as one integrated social unit. A kollektiv is not only a union or workplace council, but a community institution that manages production, municipal services, housing, education, and local culture.

Its three major levels are workshop kollektivy, factory kollektivy, and district kollektivy. The district level integrates factories with residential and social services.

== Vorkutan Model ==

The [[Vorkutan Great Reorganization]] of 1927 divided Vorkutangrad into industrial-residential districts. Each district centered on a major production facility and used assemblies to coordinate daily life, production, transport, and public services.

The [[Vorkutan Workers' Assembly]] became the city-wide coordination body. The old source presents the Vorkutan Model as an influential example of integrated worker control.

== Relationship With Orderism ==

The source says Gorodovaya Syndikalizm influenced [[Orderism]] and [[Unified Orderism]], especially their ideas about urban organization and industrial democracy.

This draft treats that as intellectual or comparative influence, not as proof that Veszpremi Orderism was founded in Vorkutangrad. Veszprem's own Orderist tradition still comes from occupation resistance, worker councils, and the [[Syndicate Revolution of 1949]].
